solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Mineral mixture in jug runs out

indicators.note: in tells us the mixture goes inside the jug once the runs have left it
out says the runs are taken away from the jug word

parts.note: a pitcher is a jug
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
a blend is a mixture

explanation.surface: Someone notices the mineral blend in their jug has all gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runs' is cricket shorthand, a single R; 'out' removes it before the mixture goes 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitchblende is a uranium-bearing ore, so a mineral by any description.

clue.text: Upset Ali, passing over boxing exercises

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the letters read upwards, backwards
boxing means the words enclose the answer, holding it like a box

explanation.surface: An upset Ali loses out on boxing as his career passes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an anagram signal but only gives letters: hidden in 'upSET ALI Passing' is SETALIP, which 'over' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilates is a regime of floor exercises for core strength and posture.

clue.text: Perhaps Rio brought up Ferguson's second figure of speech

indicators.note: brought up in a down clue means the word reads upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is an example of a port

indicators.note: second picks the second letter of the manager's name

explanation.surface: Rio Ferdinand, a footballer, is raised as an example of Alex Ferguson's second choice.
explanation.walkthrough: Rio Ferdinand played under Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United, which builds the football picture. 'brought up' makes TROP from PORT; 'second' gives E.
explanation.definitionFit: A trope is a figurative use of a word, such as a metaphor.

clue.text: Cold, like Dean compared to Declan?

definitions.meaning: cold here means unfeeling, without compassion
the name Declan with its central letters taken out becomes Dean, so Dean is Declan without a middle

explanation.surface: Two men compared, one judged the colder.
explanation.walkthrough: Cut the middle pair CL from DECLAN and DEAN is left: Dean is Declan minus its heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone without a heart lacks warmth or compassion, so is cold and unfeeling.

clue.text: Instrument — and another, not loud

indicators.note: not means the loud letter is not there, removed from the other instrument

parts.note: a flute is another instrument
F, forte, is the musical marking for loud

explanation.surface: One quiet instrument and a second one too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' drops F from FLUTE, leaving LUTE; 'another' only makes sense next to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The lute is a plucked stringed instrument with a pear-shaped body.

clue.text: Line from the other side of Watford?

definitions.meaning: the ... line is one of the London Underground lines

definitions.text: from the other side of Watford?
definitions.meaning: the north of England is dismissively called north of Watford by Londoners, so someone from beyond Watford is from the North

explanation.surface: A Tube line out past Watford.
explanation.walkthrough: Watford is a town just north of London; Londoners call the rest of England 'north of Watford'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Northern line is a Tube route, and things from the north of England are northern.

clue.text: Barman held in Kiel garrison

indicators.note: held in means the letters sit inside the run of words

explanation.surface: A man who runs a bar is kept in a German naval garrison.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden in 'KiEL GARrison'. 'Barman' is not a pub worker but a man of musical bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Elgar wrote music, so he is a man of bars of music.

clue.text: Article medical writer apparently abridged for king

parts.note: the is the definite article

indicators.note: abridged means shortened, so the writer's name loses its last letter

parts.note: Dr Seuss, the children's author, sounds like a medical doctor by his title but is not

explanation.surface: A doctor-writer's article is cut short for a king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apparently' flags that Dr Seuss is only a doctor in name. 'abridged' cuts SEUSS to SEUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Theseus was the mythical king of Athens who killed the Minotaur.

clue.text: Stick up European bank, ignoring what's outside, getting zilch

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a baton is a stick

indicators.note: ignoring what's outside means only the inside letters of bank are kept

explanation.surface: A robber holds up a European bank and leaves with nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick up' looks like a robbery but splits: 'up' reverses the stick in a down clue, and 'ignoring what's outside' strips the ends of bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Not a bean is an informal idiom for nothing at all, as is zilch.

clue.text: Act selfishly, as suggested by goalkeeper John King

parts.note: John is slang for a lavatory, a loo
after can mean in the manner of or following the lead of, as a painting is after an old master; the clue words also act out the order, lavatory and king following the keeper
a goalkeeper traditionally wears the shirt numbered one

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper called John King is accused of playing for himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Easier to see as 'John King following goalkeeper': a goalkeeper wears shirt one, John is slang for a lavatory and K is King. 'as suggested by' links the halves.
explanation.definitionFit: To put your own interests first is the idiom's sense, the very picture of acting selfishly.

clue.text: Good relationship: one might have a hand in it

definitions.text: one might have a hand in it

parts.note: a love, as in a love affair, is a romantic relationship

explanation.surface: A happy partnership in which each person plays a part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have a hand in it' reads as taking part, but it is literal: a hand goes inside this garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A glove is worn over the hand, so a hand is literally inside one.

clue.text: Either half of perfect 24

definitions.meaning: perfect eyesight is described by a hyphenated pair of identical number words, and either one fits
a cross-reference to the 24-down light, an old word for a group of that many

explanation.surface: A puzzle-like line about a perfect twenty-four.
explanation.walkthrough: '24' is not a number to work with; it points to the 24-down light, SCORE, which is twenty.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfect eyesight is called twenty-twenty, and a score is a set of twenty items.

clue.text: Want somebody wise to describe hotel by harbour failing to open

indicators.note: to describe here means to draw a line round, so the wise one encloses the rest

parts.note: a sage is a wise person
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: the harbour word loses its opening letter

parts.note: a port is a harbour

explanation.surface: A sage is wanted to write about a hotel by a harbour that won't open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to describe' is used in its geometric sense, to draw round, so the wise person encloses the hotel and the headless harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: Want in the sense of lack or scarcity is a shortage.

clue.text: Curse marred gripping finale for Jack Straw?

indicators.note: gripping means the anagram holds the extra letter in its grasp
marred means spoilt, so the letters of curse are spoilt into a new order
the finale of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: The politician Jack Straw's big finish is spoilt by a curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'marred' rearranges CURSE to SUCER, and 'gripping' puts the K that ends Jack inside it. Jack Straw is a former UK Home Secretary; here the name is split.
explanation.definitionFit: A drinking straw is something you suck through, so it is a sucker, the question mark flags it.

clue.text: Tool murderer spotted in hospital — quite the opposite

indicators.note: in, with the reversal that follows, signals one piece going inside another
quite the opposite flips the order, so the hospital goes inside the murderer rather than the reverse

parts.note: Cain killed his brother Abel in Genesis, the first murderer
saw means spotted

explanation.surface: A killer is seen in a hospital, or rather the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts the murderer in hospital; 'quite the opposite' reverses the 'in', so the hospital letter goes inside the murderer and what he did.
explanation.definitionFit: A chainsaw is a motorised cutting tool, notoriously used by horror-film killers.

clue.text: Mad Queen interrupts jokes

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so the queen goes into the middle of the jokes

parts.note: cracks are wisecracks, jokes
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: A mad queen breaks in on someone's joke-telling.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen is ER, Elizabeth Regina, a standard crossword abbreviation; 'interrupts' breaks into the jokes.
explanation.definitionFit: Crackers is British slang for crazy or out of one's mind.

clue.text: Large clubs put loner off

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

indicators.note: off means going wrong, so the letters of put loner are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Clubs are big enough to put a loner off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges PUT LONER into ORPULENT, which follows C.
explanation.definitionFit: Corpulent means fat or bulky in body, so large.

clue.text: Praise a group of underground workers finding drug

parts.note: to laud is to praise
the NUM is the National Union of Mineworkers, a British union of miners

explanation.surface: Commending a band of miners who discover drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUM is Britain's National Union of Mineworkers.
explanation.definitionFit: Laudanum is a tincture of opium, a drug once widely taken as medicine.

clue.text: Family member caught non-sailor removing prow of dinghy

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: removing says a letter is taken out of the non-sailor

parts.note: a landsman is someone who lives on land, not a seaman

indicators.note: a prow is the front of a boat, so the front letter of dinghy

explanation.surface: A landlubber gets caught out and the front of his dinghy comes off.
explanation.walkthrough: A landsman is the old word for someone who is not a seaman; 'removing' takes away the dinghy's front letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A clansman belongs to a clan, a Scottish extended family group.

clue.text: Bob's short and oddly seedy

parts.note: curt means short, brusque

indicators.note: oddly means the odd letters of seedy, first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: Bob is short and a bit shabby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a man's name but is the bob of a quick bow.
explanation.definitionFit: To bob is to make a quick dip of the knees, a polite bow.

clue.text: Satirical press about to take over Independent

indicators.note: to take over here means to take in and occupy, so the press and about hold the independent letter

parts.note: to iron is to press clothes
C, circa, means about

explanation.surface: A satirical newspaper is about to buy out the Independent, a British daily.
explanation.walkthrough: I goes between IRON and C. The Independent is a British newspaper, which is why 'press' and 'take over' feel like a media deal.
explanation.definitionFit: Irony is a mainstay of satire, so a satirical remark is ironic.

clue.text: Admit summary is being replaced by journalist

indicators.note: being replaced by says one part of the summary word is swapped for another

parts.note: summary, as an adjective, means brief or concise
ED, editor, is the standard abbreviation for a journalist

explanation.surface: A writer owns up that their summary was rewritten by a journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: In CONCISE the IS goes and ED comes in, giving CONC-ED-E.
explanation.definitionFit: To concede is to acknowledge or grant that something is so.

clue.text: The best place to be on Boxing Day?

definitions.text: The best place to be on Boxing Day?

parts.words: The best place to be on Boxing Day?
parts.note: Boxing Day is the British holiday after Christmas, but read as a day of boxing, the best seat is next to the ring

explanation.surface: Where to be on the holiday after Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxing Day, 26 December, is a British public holiday; here the capital letter is false and it means a day of boxing matches.
explanation.definitionFit: Ringside seats are right beside the boxing ring, the best view of a fight.

clue.text: Short team? In the middle, Peter Crouch!

indicators.note: short means the team word has its last letter cut off

parts.note: a squad is a team

indicators.note: in the middle picks the central letter of the name

explanation.surface: Peter Crouch, a very tall England striker, stands in the middle of a short team.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Crouch is a famously tall English footballer; the name is split here. 'Short' gives SQUA; T is Peter's middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To squat is to crouch down on one's heels.

clue.text: With temperature dropping, knock boy in river

indicators.note: dropping says the temperature letter falls out of the knock word

parts.note: a thud is a dull knock
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: As it gets colder, a boy is knocked into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With temperature dropping' reads as weather but tells you to drop T from the knock.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hudson is the major river flowing past New York City.

clue.text: Hear this result could make racehorse upset

indicators.note: upset means jumbled, so the letters of racehorse are split into hear and the answer

explanation.surface: A shock result could unsettle a racehorse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this' is the answer: HEAR plus it, jumbled, makes RACEHORSE. Subtract HEAR from RACEHORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is the final tally of a match, its result.

clue.text: The setter lifted the setter's award

indicators.note: lifted in a down clue means the word reads upwards

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me
the setter's means my, belonging to me

explanation.surface: A puzzle-setter lifts their own trophy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifted' turns ME into EM.
explanation.definitionFit: The Emmy is the American television industry's annual award.

clue.text: Who might cheer, backing United in chaos

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the cheering word is read from its end

parts.note: fans are people who might cheer
U is the abbreviation for United in football team names

explanation.surface: Supporters behind their club, Manchester United perhaps, as everything falls apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' looks like support for the club but turns the cheering people round.
explanation.definitionFit: Snafu is military slang for a situation in total confusion or disorder.

clue.text: See 9
Prepare to follow rock musical with English rock'n'roller

indicators.note: to follow puts the preparing word after the musical

parts.note: Tommy is The Who's rock opera, staged as a musical
to steel yourself is to prepare

explanation.surface: Get ready to follow a rock musical with an English rock star.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy Steele was an early British rock'n'roll star of the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: Tommy Steele was hailed as Britain's first teen rock'n'roll idol, a rock'n'roller.
